definition: Laissez-faire means favoring a hands-off approach, especially minimal government interference in markets.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word laissez-faire. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know laissez-faire should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The dorm's laissez-faire quiet-hours policy lasted exactly one midterm week.
Relaxed is the far shore from laissez-faire — the rules exist and are enforced, just gently, with the reins still firmly in hand.
Hands-off stops short of laissez-faire — a hands-off manager still watches and can step in; laissez-faire makes not interfering the official doctrine.

Permissive is about what is allowed — a permissive curfew lets much happen. Laissez-faire is about what is managed: the authority could set terms and declines, on principle, to set them. A permissive board still grants the permissions; a laissez-faire board refuses to be the gatekeeper at all.

Unregulated describes the field itself — a market or space where no rules apply at all. Laissez-faire describes the authority's stance toward the field: rules could be written, and the doctrine says leave it alone. An unregulated pond has no lifeguard chair; a laissez-faire pond keeps the chair empty on principle.

Two philosophies run the district's science fairs, and Ms.

Her approach is strictly laissez-faire: she has every power a sponsoring teacher has — to assign topics, set checkpoints, veto risky ideas — and, on principle, she uses none of it.
Her colleagues manage differently.
One approves each topic before work may begin; another checks progress weekly and nudges stragglers back on pace.
Parents sometimes mistake Ms.
Arroyo's doctrine for neglect, until they watch her at the fair, asking each student harder questions than any judge.
She knows the projects would be tidier if she steered.
She believes they would also be nobody's but hers.
